Analyst, Creator, Translator: Stop Hiring a Poet to Do an Auditor's Job

Most GenAI designs start with one decision: "Which LLM?"
Then that single model gets asked to classify tickets, route intents, translate documents and write the answers. That is not a model strategy. That is SELECT * for AI.

Transformers come in three families. Pick by workload shape, not by hype.

1. The Analyst: Encoder
Reads the full input in both directions. Every token sees every other token. The output is understanding: a label, an embedding, a span.

Examples: BERT, RoBERTa, embedding and reranker models
Fits: classification, entity extraction, intent routing, semantic search, reranking
Design trait: one forward pass, bounded output, predictable latency and cost

2. The Creator: Decoder
Reads left to right and predicts the next token, over and over. Built to continue, not to inspect.

Examples: GPT family, Claude, Llama
Fits: open-ended generation, conversation, code, reasoning, agents
Design trait: cost and latency grow with output length, and the output space is open

3. The Translator: Encoder-Decoder
The encoder digests the source completely. The decoder generates the target while attending back to it. Input in, faithful transformation out.

Examples: T5, BART, Whisper, NLLB
Fits: translation, summarization, speech-to-text, structured rewriting
Design trait: the output stays anchored to the input

Why this is an architecture decision, not model trivia:

Contract: a closed output set (say, 10 labels) is testable and governable. An open output set needs evals, guardrails and human review.
Cost: generating tokens to produce one label is paying a novelist to fill a dropdown.
Failure mode: hallucination only exists where generation exists. Do not import it into workloads that never needed it.
Separation of concerns: understanding and generation scale, fail and get monitored differently. Keep them apart and you can swap one without touching the other.

Honest caveat: a large decoder can do all three jobs through prompting, and for a prototype or low volume that is a perfectly good call. But "can" is not "should" at scale. 

Asking the Creator to do the Analyst's work is like asking your principal architect to do data entry. Technically possible. Economically hilarious.

A typical RAG pipeline uses all three roles: the Analyst embeds and reranks, the Creator writes the answer, the Translator handles multilingual input and output. Good designs compose roles instead of crowning one model.

The design principle: use the cheapest role that satisfies the output contract. Promote to the Creator only when the output is genuinely open.

A hospital can negotiate the right price for an implant and still lose the economics because the item record is wrong.

The device reaches the operating room. The scan misses. The billing code never follows.

That is the territory Symmetric Health Solutions spent 8 years learning before taking its first institutional capital. Rich Kucera, Tomás D., Jon Boerner, and Ryan Kissell founded the company in 2018 after seeing the same data problem repeatedly in healthcare supply-chain work. They bootstrapped the business, kept it profitable, and built a maintained product-data layer for hospitals that were tired of paying for records their own teams still had to repair.

Spectrum Equity is now making a strategic growth investment in Symmetric. The amount was not disclosed. Spectrum is backing a product that sits beneath purchasing, contracts, recalls, substitutions, charge capture, ERP performance, and hospital AI projects.

Hospital item masters can contain more than 500,000 rows, while products, packaging, reimbursement codes, contract terms, suppliers, and classifications keep changing. Symmetric reconciles that movement across regulatory registries, manufacturer catalogs, GPO contracts, and other sources, then pushes maintained records into systems such as Workday, Oracle, and Infor.

The company and investor report nearly 20M healthcare items, as many as 1,800 attributes per item, 5M verified substitutes, a 96% average match rate, and staff at more than 45 health systems contributing verification. Symmetric also says 98% of customers have stayed since founding. Those are company-reported metrics, but they describe why the data layer becomes harder to replace once operating teams trust it.

Spectrum's capital will support product development, hiring, go-to-market, and customer success. Symmetric is expanding Contract Management, already used by more than 1 in 5 customers, while building a supply-chain control tower, revenue-integrity tools, value analysis, and a supplier portal.

The opportunity is larger than cleaning a catalog. Hospitals want AI to forecast disruption, protect margin, automate procurement, and guide clinical substitutions. Those systems will inherit every ambiguity underneath them. Symmetric's growth phase will be decided by whether it can keep the record trustworthy while more customers, products, contracts, and decisions begin depending on it.

Most teams pick the wrong workflow to automate first, then decide "AI agents don't work."

They aim the agent at the hardest, fuzziest, highest-stakes task in the building, and are surprised when it flops.

Here is the test I would run before building anything. A workflow is ready for an agent if:

• It happens often.
• You can write down the steps.
• Software can reach everything it needs.
• You can tell if it was done right.
• A mistake is survivable.

The more of those you can answer yes to, the better the fit. If it is rare, if the logic is "you just know," if the context lives in people's heads, or if one mistake is catastrophic, it is not ready yet.

And one of those five matters more than the rest: can you tell if it was done right? Every other trait has a workaround. This one does not. If you cannot check the output, you cannot trust it, and you cannot improve it.

In practice, here is the split:

Ready today: tier-1 support answered from your docs, enriching and scoring inbound leads, invoice and receipt data entry, triaging incoming tickets, summarizing calls into the CRM.

Not yet: negotiating a major contract, the final hiring decision, a sensitive complaint, signing off on large payments, one-off strategic calls.

Start where it is boring and safe. Nail that, build trust, then move up to the harder calls.

What is the first workflow you would hand to an agent, and does it pass the test?

We might have just lost a potential client. And surprisingly, I don't think it was a bad outcome.

It started when my co-founder met someone from a manufacturing company at a business event.
One conversation led to another, and soon we were discussing a fairly ambitious AI implementation.

We were excited.

The client had a clear vision of what they wanted, and we say an opportunity to demonstrate what Everyse Solutions could do.

So we started building a tailored Proof of Concept.

Not a fully deployed system. A working demo to show how AI employees could operate within their business workflows.

There was one catch.

The client wanted to see it before the end of the month. We had roughly 20 days, and some of the operational data we needed to tailor the demo was still pending.

Meanwhile, the scope being discussed had grown far beyond the early price indication we'd given.
We were willing to invest the effort because we believe in the opportunity.
But during our latest meeting, the conversation took an unexpected turn.
They were considering hiring someone internally to build the system instead.

And that's when something clicked for me.

AI has made building software look incredibly easy. But there's a difference between making something work once and making something work reliably inside a business.

A demo can show what AI is capable of.
A production system has to deal with real data, integrations, exceptions, permissions, failures, and people depending on it every day.


Especially when you're building AI employees that don't just answer questions, but actually execute work.
We may not end up working together, and that's okay.
Because we walked away with something valuable.

A much deeper understanding of another manufacturing operation, reusable components from the PoC, and a better understanding of how to set expectation before discussing commercial commitments.

Sometimes the most valuable thing you get from a potential client isn't the contract. It's a clearer understanding of what you're actually building.

And the best part? The work didn't go to waste.
We now have a working PoC that we're excited to keep developing.
If you're in manufacturing and curious about what AI employees could actually do inside your operations, my DMs are open.

I'd love to show you what we've built, hear how things work at your factory, and explore what's possible together.
You might be surprised by how much AI can already take off your team's plate.

My two cents on the current market: 

AI demand is accelerating quickly. Job ads requiring AI capability have roughly doubled over the past year, with AI skills now appearing across a significant proportion of software and data roles.

AI Engineers are a clear example, with demand reportedly up around 150%. The supply of people with genuine hands-on AI experience simply isn’t keeping up.

That shortage is creating a new tier of candidate. People who can genuinely build and implement AI are commanding strong packages, with some offers now including access to AI tooling and tokens.

We’re also seeing experienced technical leaders getting back into the code. Even CTO-level candidates are exploring Software Engineering roles because they want to be hands-on with AI.

At the same time, the broader tech market feels much quieter.

The traditional domino effect of hiring has slowed down. When someone leaves, organisations are increasingly choosing to absorb the workload and “do more with less”.

Job flow has slowed, salaries and contract rates have flattened, and junior and mid-level opportunities continue to decline as AI takes on tasks that previously helped develop less experienced engineers.

However, specialist expertise remains highly valued. When businesses need niche technical knowledge or a specific capability delivered quickly, they’re still prepared to pay for it.

Your multi-agent system won't fail in the demo. It will fail in month two, when real customers and real money are involved.
If you lead an AI team or hire AI engineers, this is the gap that costs the most.
I studied a 20-concept breakdown of how production agents are built. The multi-agent layer showed me what separates a demo builder from a senior AI engineer. Here's what I learned:
𝟭. 𝗔𝗴𝗲𝗻𝘁𝘀 𝗻𝗲𝗲𝗱 𝗮 𝗺𝗮𝗻𝗮𝗴𝗲𝗿, 𝗻𝗼𝘁 𝗷𝘂𝘀𝘁 𝗺𝗼𝗿𝗲 𝗮𝗴𝗲𝗻𝘁𝘀.
Five agents don't automatically work well together. A real team has one coordinator who plans and assigns the work, and specialists who do it. Build one orchestrator and give the tools to a researcher and a tester. For your business, this means clear ownership of every task and fewer surprises. It also makes the system easier to scale as you add more agents. When you interview AI engineers, ask them how they design this.
𝟮. 𝗔𝗴𝗲𝗻𝘁𝘀 𝘀𝗵𝗼𝘂𝗹𝗱 𝘁𝗮𝗹𝗸 𝗶𝗻 𝗮 𝗳𝗶𝘅𝗲𝗱 𝗳𝗼𝗿𝗺𝗮𝘁.
Air traffic control never speaks casually with pilots, and your agents shouldn't either. Vague messages between agents lead to errors that are very hard to trace. Keep natural language, but carry it inside structured fields: task, status, inputs, outputs and errors. This makes systems easier to debug, audit and hand over to a new team member.
𝟯. 𝗢𝗻𝗲 𝗰𝗼𝗻𝗳𝗶𝗱𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗮𝗴𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗶𝘀 𝗮 𝗯𝘂𝘀𝗶𝗻𝗲𝘀𝘀 𝗿𝗶𝘀𝗸.
A single agent can be wrong and still sound sure. Add a critic agent that checks the builder's work, like a code reviewer, and add human approval for high-risk actions. Refunds, contracts and customer data should never depend on one unchecked answer. This one layer protects your money and your reputation.
𝟰. 𝗦𝗵𝗮𝗿𝗲𝗱 𝘀𝘁𝗮𝘁𝗲 𝘀𝗮𝘃𝗲𝘀 𝗰𝗼𝘀𝘁 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝘁𝗶𝗺𝗲.
Don't make every agent reread a long chat. Keep one simple board with IDs, status, decisions and pending work, for example in Redis. Each agent picks up only what it needs. Fewer tokens means lower cost and faster answers, and that shows up directly on your monthly bill.
𝟱. 𝗝𝘂𝗱𝗴𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗿𝗼𝘂𝘁𝗲, 𝗻𝗼𝘁 𝗷𝘂𝘀𝘁 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗮𝗻𝘀𝘄𝗲𝗿.
An agent can reach the right result with too many steps, retries and cost. Evaluate the whole path (DeepEval is a good start), and trace every call with OpenTelemetry, like a black box on an aircraft. When something breaks, you will know where and why, and your team gets clear answers instead of guesses. That is what makes a system ready for production.
The takeaway:
Anyone can build an agent that works once. The real value is in building one that works every day and can be trusted.
Which would worry you more in your own team: unchecked agent actions or cost you can't explain?

Mastering the DMAIC Define Phase: A Guide for Black Belts 🥇

The Define Phase is the critical foundation of any Lean Six Sigma project. It is not merely about selecting a problem; it is about rigorously scoping it, validating its impact, and setting the stage for success. If the Define phase is weak, the entire project will suffer from scope creep, lack of clarity, and misaligned resources.

As a Black Belt, your role in this phase is to act as a project leader and a change agent, ensuring that the business case is sound and that the team is aligned on what "success" looks like.

Here are the primary objectives of the Define Phase:
🎯Identify the problem and its impact.
🎯Define the scope and boundaries.
🎯Map the high-level process.
🎯Identify key stakeholders and the project team.

Secure project authorization (Project Charter).
1. The Core Inputs and Tools
To begin the Define phase, you need specific inputs and must deploy the right toolkit.
Key Inputs:
☘️Voice of the Business (VOB): Strategic goals, financial imperatives, and high-level metrics (e.g., "We are losing market share due to late deliveries").
☘️Voice of the Customer (VOC): Customer feedback, complaints, and requirements (e.g., "Customers expect delivery within 3 days").
Essential Define Phase Tools:
☘️Project Charter: The foundational contract for the project.
☘️SIPOC Diagram: A high-level process map (Suppliers, Inputs, Process, Outputs, Customers).
☘️Voice of the Customer (VOC) Analysis: Translating raw customer feedback into critical requirements.
Stakeholder Analysis: Mapping influence and interest levels of affected parties.
2. Developing the Project Charter: Your Contract for Success
The Project Charter is the most important output of the Define phase. It is a living document that must be reviewed and approved by the Project Sponsor. A robust charter prevents "scope creep" and ensures everyone is aligned.
Critical Elements of a Project Charter:
☘️Business Case: Why are we doing this project? What is the pain (financial or otherwise) if we don't do it? Tip: Use hard financial data (cost of poor quality - COPQ) to justify the project.
☘️Problem Statement: A concise, quantifiable description of the problem. It should answer: What is wrong? Where is it happening? When did it start? What is the magnitude of the defect?
☘️Goal Statement (SMART): What does success look like? The goal must be Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, and Time-bound (e.g., "Reduce the defect rate from 5% to 1% by December 31st").
☘️Project Scope: Clearly defines what is "In Scope" and, equally important, what is "Out of Scope."
☘️Timeline & Milestones: High-level schedule linked to the DMAIC tollgates.
☘️Team & Resources: Who is on the team, and what is their time commitment? Who is the Process Owner?

Hi, I'm Daniel Goodrich, and this is the story of how I built a law firm designed for founders, by founders.

SCENE: 2006. NYC. A young intern at his tiny desk at a record label. 

11:00 AM on a Wednesday, I heard champagne bottles popping down the hall. We'd just signed a new rapper. I was busy answering phone calls.

That was the moment I knew the music industry wasn't my path.

I'd fallen in love with hip-hop growing up in New York, and chased a career tangential to music because it felt like the closest I'd get to doing what I loved. So I took jobs and internships at record labels, thinking that was my way in.

It wasn't. 

I was a glorified executive assistant, watching other people close the deals I wanted to be part of.

That Wednesday, I asked my boss how he did what he did and how I could get there myself.
 
He gave me two options: climb the ladder for years, or go to law school and come back as an agent.

Law school won, and I set out to buy myself more time to figure things out in the middle of a terrible economy.

What I didn't expect was to fall into startups instead. 

I was on the founding team of a renewable energy company at 24 and General Counsel of a healthcare startup at 28. 

Of course, none of it came with a playbook. We were figuring out contracts, hiring, and cash flow at the same time, while juggling all the other hats that never made it to our resumes. 

Across all my years working in and building startups, I saw founders struggle with the same challenge:

Legal always felt like the last thing founders wanted to think about, and the first thing that could sink them. 

So I built @VirtualCounsel to fix that.

Our best-fit clients enjoy a predictable subscription model — unlimited communication, no bill for picking up the phone or sending an email. You get a dedicated attorney who actually knows your business, and the whole team to back you up. Intentionally intimate team, real access, and no handing off your account to the next junior associate.

On this page, I'll be writing about what I see working alongside founders:
- the legal mistakes people make before they ever call an attorney
- where AI is quietly creating more problems than it solves in contracts and fundraising docs
- and a few fun stories from a career that took a lot of detours to get here.

If you're building something and tired of legal feeling like a mysterious monster you're supposed to just deal with, you're in the right place.

But it is going to change my job. And I'm perfectly fine with that.

AI can research destinations.

Summarize hotel information.

Compare documents.

Organize requirements.

And probably save planners hours of work every week.

I'm using it too…

But here's where I think the distinction matters.

Information has never been the most valuable part of hotel sourcing.

Judgment is.

AI can tell you that Hotel A has 40,000 square feet of meeting space.

It can't tell you that I've worked with that hotel before and know exactly which questions to ask about how that space operates for a group like yours.

It can summarize a proposal.

It doesn't have a 20-year relationship with the person on the other side of the negotiation.

It can identify a contract clause.

It doesn't know what I've successfully negotiated around that clause with similar properties and programs.

And it can't walk into a hotel and notice the small operational details that tell me whether I trust that property with 300 of my client's people.

AI is an incredible tool, and I plan to keep using it.

But after 30+ years in this business, what my clients are hiring me for isn't information they could find faster with technology.

It's knowing what that information actually means.

Planners, where is AI making your job easier right now?
